action_criteria.expected_evidence: MoCA 20/30 with delayed recall 0/5 with minimal gain on category cue (1/5) or multiple choice (2/5), Epworth 18/24 and Apathy Evaluation Scale 54, with naming, repetition and fluency preserved
action_criteria.label: Perform a validated bedside cognitive assessment and record the per-domain profile and whether delayed recall improves with cueing
action_criteria.rationale: Five months of amnesia, sleepiness and apathy after an abrupt event must be measured on a validated instrument, including whether recall responds to cues, before it is attributed [VASCOG_2014].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: RAVLT learning, delayed recall and recognition at or below the 1st percentile with confabulation and impaired sustained attention, against normal letter fluency, naming and digit span
action_criteria.label: Order formal multi-domain neuropsychological testing to settle the executive-versus-amnestic attribution and to document a baseline for follow-up
action_criteria.rationale: Formal testing characterises the amnesia (storage versus retrieval) that the screen cannot separate from drowsiness, and documents a baseline for her occupational assessment [VASCOG_2014].

action_criteria.label: Order the reversible-cause screen and the vascular-risk assays that will be treated (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate, RPR, HIV, HbA1c, lipid panel)
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes reversible contributors to the amnesia and measures the lipid and glycaemic targets of secondary prevention after her infarct [AAN_MCI_2018] [AHA_ASA_2011_VCI].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Chronic bilateral paramedian thalamic and rostral midbrain infarcts in the artery of Percheron territory, about 1.6 mL, with Fazekas 1 change, no microbleeds and normal hippocampi (MTA 0)
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI reported in STRIVE-2 terms (FLAIR with Fazekas grade, T1/T2 for infarcts and lacunes, DWI for lesion age, SWI for microbleeds and siderosis) with the medial temporal atrophy grade
action_criteria.rationale: A CT at the index admission was normal; MRI is the study that can show small thalamic and midbrain infarcts and make the vascular attribution [STRIVE_2] [VASCOG_2014].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal sinus rhythm, rate 72, normal intervals, no left ventricular hypertrophy
action_criteria.label: Obtain a 12-lead ECG for atrial fibrillation after the ischaemic infarct
action_criteria.rationale: An ECG is part of the work-up of every ischaemic stroke, and an artery of Percheron occlusion can be embolic [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No stenosis of the basilar artery, basilar tip, P1 segments or cervical arteries; the perforators themselves are below MRA resolution
action_criteria.label: Obtain MR angiography of the head and neck for posterior-circulation stenosis or dissection
action_criteria.rationale: A posterior-circulation infarct calls for vessel imaging of the basilar tip and P1 segments, from which the Percheron artery arises, to exclude a large-artery mechanism [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: LVEF 60%, mild concentric hypertrophy, normal left atrium, no thrombus or vegetation
action_criteria.label: Obtain a transthoracic echocardiogram for a cardioembolic source
action_criteria.rationale: A single occlusion at the origin of a perforator supplying both thalami may be embolic; TTE is reasonable to look for a source [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: 14 days of sinus rhythm with no atrial fibrillation or flutter
action_criteria.label: Obtain prolonged ambulatory rhythm monitoring for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
action_criteria.rationale: With a normal ECG and no other mechanism shown, prolonged monitoring is reasonable to exclude paroxysmal atrial fibrillation [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Zolpidem 10 mg is a drug to avoid at her age and with cognitive impairment, above the labelled dose for women; the antiplatelet to be started has no interaction of note with her medicines
action_criteria.label: Review zolpidem and the antiplatelet to be started against her current medicines
action_criteria.rationale: She takes a hypnotic that worsens sleepiness and memory, and will need an antiplatelet after the infarct; a medication review supports both decisions.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not accept a normal CT as excluding bilateral paramedian thalamic infarction
Do not prescribe or continue a hypnotic in a patient with hypersomnolence from a diencephalic lesion and a dense amnesia
Do not carry forward a diagnosis of 'encephalopathy of uncertain cause' when a fixed anatomical syndrome is present
Do not rely on the patient's own account when apathy and amnesia are both present
Do not clear her to return to dispensing medication without formal occupational assessment
required_recommendations: Recognise that a fixed deficit five months after an abrupt event is a structural lesion, not a resolved encephalopathy
Interpret the vertical gaze palsy with preserved vestibulo-ocular reflex as supranuclear, localising with the hypersomnolence and the amnesia to the paramedian thalami and rostral midbrain
Recognise that paramedian thalamic infarcts are often invisible on CT in the acute phase, which is why the index admission was labelled an encephalopathy
Treat as a small perforator infarct: start a single antiplatelet (aspirin 75-100 mg or clopidogrel 75 mg daily) [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary]
Increase atorvastatin from 20 mg to high intensity (80 mg) for LDL 106 mg/dL after an ischaemic stroke [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary]
Lower blood pressure (146/84 mmHg on candesartan) gradually to below 130/80 mmHg, checking orthostatic BP at each change [AHA_ASA_2021_secondary]
Stop zolpidem, which worsens both the hypersomnolence and the amnesia and is a drug to avoid at her age
Arrange supervised medication administration, since she cannot remember whether she has taken her tablets
Address the occupational risk explicitly: she dispensed medication and cannot do so with this deficit; advise her not to drive

avoided_actions.rationale: The deficit has been fixed since a single abrupt event five months ago, with no fluctuation, seizure or progression, and she rouses fully to voice; EEG would not change the diagnosis.
No parkinsonism, fluctuating cognition, hallucinations or dream enactment; a dopamine transporter scan does not address her syndrome.
No Lewy body features or autonomic failure; cardiac sympathetic imaging does not address her syndrome.
An abrupt single event followed by a fixed deficit without subacute progression is not the indication for a paraneoplastic or autoimmune encephalitis battery.
MRI is available and not contraindicated; CT cannot show microbleeds, siderosis or small lacunes, and missed these thalamic infarcts at the index admission.

accepted: Vascular dementia — strategic infarct type, bilateral paramedian thalamic and rostral midbrain infarction in the artery of Percheron territory

differential.key_features: The discharge diagnosis, which survived because the acute CT was normal; a fixed deficit five months later with a supranuclear vertical gaze palsy, a storage amnesia and chronic bilateral thalamic and midbrain infarcts on MRI is an anatomical lesion, not a resolved metabolic disturbance

differential.diagnosis: Idiopathic hypersomnia or a sleep disorder
differential.key_features: The hypnotic prescribed at discharge treats this hypothesis, but hypersomnolence with full arousability, a storage amnesia, a vertical gaze palsy and bilateral paramedian thalamic infarcts on MRI is a diencephalic lesion, and zolpidem can only worsen it
Onset was abrupt on a single day with no progression in five months, the hippocampi are entirely normal and language and working memory are preserved
A vertical gaze palsy with apathy overlaps, but onset was abrupt, there is no axial rigidity, no falls, no midbrain atrophy, and there has been no progression

Confabulation and amnesia overlap, but there is no alcohol or nutritional risk, no nuclear ophthalmoparesis or ataxia, the mamillary bodies are normal on MRI and the lesions are chronic infarcts in one arterial territory

key_clinical_evidence: The triad localises: hypersomnolence, a dense storage amnesia and a supranuclear vertical gaze palsy together point to the paramedian thalami and rostral midbrain, and the artery of Percheron is the vessel that supplies all three in one territory
A single anatomical variant explains a bilateral lesion from a single occlusion, which is why the syndrome looks diffuse and is in fact focal
1.6 mL of tissue produced a dementia — the strategic principle in its clearest form, because the dorsomedial nuclei and mamillothalamic tracts carry the memory circuit bilaterally
CT misses paramedian thalamic infarcts, and a normal CT is what allowed five months and an inappropriate hypnotic to intervene
Preserved arousability distinguishes a diencephalic hypersomnolence from a reduced level of consciousness, and it is what makes this a chronic focal syndrome rather than an encephalopathy

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Paramedian thalamic infarcts are characteristically invisible on CT; the MRI shows chronic bilateral thalamic and midbrain infarction dating to that admission

red_herrings.intended_effect: Reframes the syndrome as a primary sleep disorder and adds a drug that worsens both the sleepiness and the amnesia

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Beatrice Sartori is a 66-year-old hospital pharmacy technician who five months ago became profoundly drowsy and confused over the course of an hour at work. She was admitted, a CT of the head was reported as normal, routine bloods and a toxicology screen were unremarkable, and after three days of gradual improvement she was discharged with a diagnosis of probable encephalopathy of uncertain cause and a hypnotic for presumed sleep disturbance. Her husband reports that she has never returned to normal. She sleeps twelve to fourteen hours a night and dozes repeatedly during the day, but rouses immediately and fully when spoken to. She cannot retain anything new: she asks the same question repeatedly, cannot remember whether she has taken her tablets, and has twice told her daughter news she had been told the day before as though it were fresh. She is strikingly unconcerned about all of it. She has not returned to work, where she dispensed medication. Her husband has also noticed that she 'does not look up' — she cannot see items on a high shelf without tilting her head. There has been no further abrupt event, no headache, no weakness, no hallucinations and no dream enactment.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Hypersomnolent: fell asleep twice during the consultation when not engaged, rousing immediately and fully to voice. Oriented to person and place; year correct, month and date incorrect. Answers slowly, conversation coherent. Mild confabulation about the previous week. Marked apathy. Formal cognitive screening reported separately.
